title: Single-Stage Amplifiers
intro: Complex amplifiers are built from four basic stages: common source, source follower, common gate and cascode. Learn each stage's gain, input and output impedance and headroom.

blocks.text: A signal is amplified because it is too small to drive a load, to rise above the noise of the next stage, or to reach logic levels. A phone shows the variety: a low-noise amplifier (LNA) right after the antenna, more gain stages down the receive chain (all while strong unwanted signals arrive alongside the weak wanted one), and a power amplifier that drives the antenna on the transmit side and takes most of the battery's energy.

An ideal amplifier is linear, $y(t) = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 x(t)$, where $\alpha_0$ is the bias point and $\alpha_1$ the gain. Real circuits bend as the signal moves the bias point, which is modelled by a polynomial:

Besides gain and speed, power, supply voltage, linearity, noise, swing and input/output impedance all matter, and they trade against each other (the analog design octagon). Each stage needs two analyses: biasing, so every device has the right current and $V_{DS}$ (treated in Current Mirrors and Biasing), and the large- and small-signal response around that bias point, which is this chapter.

blocks.alt: An octagon whose eight corners are labelled gain, speed, power dissipation, supply voltage, linearity, noise, input/output impedance and voltage swings, with thin lines joining every pair of corners.
blocks.caption: The analog design octagon. Every stage in this chapter is a different compromise between these eight.

items: Common source (the workhorse): resistive, diode-connected, current-source, active (complementary) and triode loads; with source degeneration.
Source follower (voltage buffer): biased by a resistor or a current source.
Common gate (current buffer, low input resistance): resistive or current-source load.
Cascode (high output resistance): telescopic or folded.

blocks.text: Three resistances, derived on the subpages, let you write the gain of most circuits without drawing a small-signal model. With $\lambda = \gamma = 0$ the source looks like $1/g_m$; in general:

items: Looking into the gate: infinite at low frequency.
Looking into the drain, with $R_S$ from source to ground: $[1 + (g_m + g_{mb})r_o]R_S + r_o$. The transistor multiplies its source resistance by roughly its intrinsic gain.

Looking into the source, with $R_D$ from drain to an AC ground: $\frac{R_D + r_o}{1 + (g_m + g_{mb})r_o} \approx \frac{1}{g_m + g_{mb}} + \frac{R_D}{(g_m + g_{mb})r_o}$. The transistor divides its drain resistance by roughly its intrinsic gain.

Gain of a stage: $A_v = -G_m R_{out}$, with $G_m$ the short-circuit transconductance and $R_{out}$ the output resistance (proved on the Source Degeneration page). For a CS-like stage, $|A_v|$ is the resistance seen at the drain divided by the resistance in the source path, $\frac{1}{g_m} + R_S$.

blocks.alt: Two circuits. Left: transistor M1 with gate at AC ground and resistor RS from source to ground; an arrow labelled R up points at the drain terminal. Right: transistor M1 with gate at a bias voltage Vb and resistor RD from drain to VDD; an arrow labelled R down points at the source terminal.
blocks.caption: Impedance transformation: a MOSFET scales source resistance up when seen from the drain, and drain resistance down when seen from the source.

blocks.text: Ask what each side of the stage connects to. A high-impedance source that must not be loaded needs a gate input (CS or follower). A low-impedance or current-mode source wants a low input resistance (CG). Driving a heavy load at unity gain calls for a follower; maximizing gain calls for the highest output resistance (cascode). Most larger circuits are combinations of these.

items: Break the circuit into familiar stages.
Start with the simplest model, a current source $g_m v_{gs}$, for every saturated device. Add $r_o$ only where a drain sees a high impedance (for example another drain).
In a second pass, add body effect for devices whose source is not at AC ground.
For bias calculations, ignore $\lambda$ and $\gamma$ at first and add them once the basic operating point makes sense.
Then simulate: short-channel devices cannot be predicted accurately by hand, but without the hand analysis you cannot judge whether the simulation is right.

blocks.title: Pick the stage
blocks.text: You need to drive a $50\,\Omega$ load from a high-impedance sensor with a voltage gain of about 1 and little loading of the sensor. Which stage fits, and what does it cost?
solution: A source follower: its gate does not load the sensor and its output resistance is about $1/(g_m + g_{mb})$.

To make that small next to $50\,\Omega$ needs $g_m$ well above 20 mS, i.e. a large device and a large bias current. Even then the gain is only about 0.5 when $1/g_m = R_L$; for a given current a CS stage with the load as its drain resistor would give more gain (see the Source Follower page).
blocks.answer: A source follower (buffer), at the price of a large bias current.

blocks.title: Two resistances by inspection
blocks.text: A transistor has $g_m = 2\text{ mS}$, $g_{mb} = 0$ and $r_o = 20\text{ k}\Omega$. (a) With $1\text{ k}\Omega$ from source to ground, what resistance is seen at the drain? (b) With $10\text{ k}\Omega$ from drain to $V_{DD}$, what is seen at the source?
solution: (a) $[1 + g_m r_o]R_S + r_o = (1 + 40)(1\text{ k}\Omega) + 20\text{ k}\Omega = 61\text{ k}\Omega$.
(b) $\frac{R_D + r_o}{1 + g_m r_o} = \frac{30\text{ k}\Omega}{41} \approx 732\,\Omega$, somewhat above $1/g_m = 500\,\Omega$.
